# **<u>Copper BRIEFING SERVICE</u>** 

## **April 2012** 







#### When Liquid Stocks are Not So Liquid…. 

Exchange and merchant stocks running higher 

- ….as imports into China surge 

….and spot premia outside China rise 

The market in Q1 2012 is seriously in surplus 

##### …. but should move back into deficit in Q2 

We look at “liquid stocks” to indicate how physical market fundamentals are played out in prac-ce. The liquid stocks figure is intended to reflect the amount of refined copper that is available for purchase by consumers. High liquid stocks should reflect a market that is perceived to be over supplied, and vice versa. We include in our liquid stocks figure exchange stocks, merchant bonded stocks and other in-country material not in strategic reserve and not strictly needed as pipeline inventory, minus copper covered by ETFs. 

So much for the theory. In prac-ce, liquid stock data can only be a market indicator; actual availability of copper can deviate enormously. This is the case right now, a fact that goes a long way towards explaining why prices remain high when liquid stocks, as we define them, have increased drama-cally in the first quarter of 2012. 

For Q1, we see a market that has moved sharply into surplus, as Chinese copper use falters and, elsewhere, demand picks up only slowly. We see the surplus as being closely reflected in a build up in liquid stocks of about 175 kt. According to our figures, liquid stocks have grown from 3.6 weeks of copper use in Q4 2011 to 4.1 weeks this in Q1 2012. Most of the build up is in merchant bonded stocks, but total exchange and abnormal country stocks have also grown. Why then, con-nued high copper prices? 

One factor is the huge reloca-on of stock to China. Although total exchange inventories rose slightly in Q1 2012, this misses the fact that there was a big drawdown outside China (of 118 kt), and a huge increase on the SHFE (of 132 kt). The same is true of non-pipeline inventories, which have become even more depleted in Europe and the United States while growing significantly in China. Add to this the fact that the rise in merchant bonded stock is almost en-rely China-based, then we see the massive gap between the market as it appears in China and how it appears in the rest of the world. In Europe in par-cular, be-er than expected consump-on has meant a scramble by some consumers to cover their needs that were not met by term contracts. The story in the US is more complicated, as apparently available 



exchange stock proves not to be so for material -ed up in physical trader deals. Even in China, supposedly liquid merchant bonded stock may not be so if held for financing purposes, as most appears to be. 

The net result is that there is visible -ghtness in copper in some parts of the world, despite rising “liquid stocks”. This is reflected in high spot premia and nearby backwarda-on, and in high overall copper pricing. With prices higher than we think they should be, we ma

### Prices, Market Balance and Stocks 

##### Strong Pricing Belies Market Weakness 

Despite the slide into market surplus in Q1 2012, copper pricing has remained robust. LME Cash started March at its highest point this year, at $8,625/t. Having slipped in the next week to below $8,300/t, in the past few days we have seen a rebound to over $8,550/t, boosted by German manufacturer confidence data and the prospect of monetary easing in the United States. As for the LME forward curve, in the past week or so LME Cash to 3-month copper has been showing a solid $30-40/t backwarda-on. Meanwhile, LME 3-month to 15-month copper is now virtually flat; LME 15-month to 27-month is recording a backwarda-on of $50-80/t. 

LME prices have performed be-er than those on the Shanghai exchange. For March to date, S

HFE 1-month copper has been just 11.6% above LME Cash on average, slipping to near 10% in recent days. This is well below the level where we might expect to see strong imports into China on pure price grounds. ##### Liquid Stocks on the Increase The main components of liquid stock are exchange inventories and merchant bonded stocks. Over the past month, total exchange inventories have been falling slightly, a net loss of around 30 kt masking a small gain in China and a larger fall elsewhere. Any change in exchange stocks, however, is en-rely dwarfed by a huge increase in merchant bonded stocks, located almost en-rely in China. Material in Chinese nonexchange bonded warehouses is thought to have increased from less than 400 kt at the end of February to around 650 kt today, a 250 kt increase. This indicates that what may typically be regarded as liquid stocks have risen drama-cally in March. Exchange Stocks by Location

##### Spot Premia Reflect Disloca-on in Stocks Rising liquid stocks normally mean lower pricing and, in par-cular, lower spot cathode premia. Neither in fact apply in today’s market. One reason for this is the huge concentra-on of liquid stock in China, both on the exchange and in merchant hands. Outside China, liquid stocks are running very low indeed in Europe. Here, spot premia for a good brand of cathode cif Ro-erdam have increased to around $90/t. Despite large tonnages on the exchanges in the United States, premia are high here also. Some reports suggest that a some of US exchange stocks are not suitable for all consumers because of a high bismuth content, but s-ll, it had appeared earlier this year that a sharp drawdown was imminent. This an-cipated reduc-on gives more room to allow a slow down if needed while the government carries out promised economic and welfare reforms ahead of a leadership transi-on, due later this year. If the growth figure finally comes in a 7.5%, it would be the lowest rate since 1990. However, It is not a secret that Beijing’s GDP target acts more as a benchmark floor rather than a ceiling, as the previous 8% “target” has been repeatedly exceeded. Mr Wen puts as top priority for 2012 a boost to consumer demand while keeping infla-on stable and money supply and credit at an “appropriate” level. Policies to "encourage consump-on" are expected to have a posi-ve effect on commodi-es in China and in neighbouring countries reliant on Chinese demand. At the same -me. the Central Bank has stated that it will allow the value of yuan to be set by the market and step back from interven-on "in an orderly manner". This statement came days a-er China reported a surprise US$13.5 billion trade deficit for February resul-ng from a sharp decline in export markets.. Despite uncertain performance in China, global IP has done be-er than expected, rising by 0.6% in January. OECD output alone increased by 0.7%. March flash PMI for China fell to 48.1, down from a final reading of 49.6 in February. Following improvements in Europe and the US in February, Europe’s March flash PME was disappoin-ng at 48.8 (down 1.5 points). OECD and non-OECD Industrial Production

### Consump-on Trends Although official figures indicate strong growth, Chinese copper consump-on is evidently not performing well. Fabricator plant u-lisa-on ranges 5070%, compared to near full u-lisa-on at this -me last year. Admi-edly, in part this reflect capacity growth, but the signs are not encouraging. Par-cular concern surrounds high inventory levels of both fabricated products and finished manufactures, especially air condi-oners. End-2011 stocks of unsold air condi-oners

stood at 11.9 million units, leading to a 22% cut in output in January alone. Automo-ve output was also down, by 1.8% year on year in in JanuaryFebruary. Further government s-mulus to domes-c consump-on and limited growth in infrastructure investment should help the Chinese market later this year, but with a weak private construc-on market, lacklustre manufacturing and high inventories, we are unlikely to see anything but modest copper market growth in China in coming months. But, for the year as a whole, some domes-c observers are quite bullish. Tongling forecasts 6% market growth for 2012, while Jiangxi Copper forecasts 7%, based largely on growth in affordable housing and power network investment. Copper products company Luvata expects that firm growth in HVACR, renewable energy and healthcare will li- its sales volume by 5% this year. For Japan, the mill products industry associa-on forecasts be-er demand for all major items bar copper tube. As for the cable sector, new subsidies for eco-friendly cars are expected to boost demand for auto wire. Smelter grade capacity includes a small amount of low grade electrowon 8 **© Copyright: Photocopying and Electronic Forwarding Prohibited Email: reports@intierra.com** ### Produc-on Trends ##### Expanding Mine Output, Growing Surpluses? It is nearly two years now that we have been looking at a copper market that is structurally -ght, but which threatens to become much less so as new mine capacity comes to overwhelm demand. This s-ll is the underlying picture, but the detail of the scene has changed. While the project list gets ever longer and deeper, so does the -me when the new capacity is supposed to arrive extend outwards to a later date. Moreover, even as we approach the period when new projects are supposed to be coming on stream, mine output has resolutely failed to impress. The shor-all in mine output was very evident in 201

1. This was mainly because of low produc-on at some of copper’s biggest mines. With just 0.6% growth, mine output in 2011 fell below even the most pessimis-c of predic-ons. It has come to be acknowledged that mine output is likely to come in at around 5% below (overop-mis-c) plans at the start of the year. But, with over 6% “disrup-on” in 2011, this was an excep-onal year. For 2012 a rebound is expected from the very meagre output of 2011. However, the start of the year has hardly been encouraging. Codelco, one of the few major producers to report an increase in output in 2011, has already made it clear that it will have trouble matching last year’s performance due to lower grades. Chile’s mine output overall in January was reported to be down by 8% year on year, while Peruvian January output was down by 5%. As for Freeport, affected by on going industrial unrest at Grasberg in Indonesia (now resolved), its expected output for Q1 2012 is 36.3 kt less than in previous guidance. There is a general expecta-on that mine output will start to ramp up in the second half of 2012. This may be true, but the increase could be quite small. In the table below we show greenfield and brownfield capacity expansions for 2012 to 2014, taken from our “Copper Quarterly” database. Here, we make some judgement as to project slippage. Based on these figures, we es-mate the total increment to capacity in 2012 from projects that will each give over 20 ktpy capacity expansion at 804 ktpy. Brownfield expansions, of which Los Bronces in Chile is the biggest, will be almost as important as greenfield projects, amongst which first produc-on at Salobo and Antapaccay and ramp up at Esperanza and Copper Mountain are the most significant. The expansions proposed for 2012 are hardly stunning, although higher than in recent years. The same could be said for 2013 and 2014, despite the entry of such major projects as Oyu Tolgoi, Sierra Gorda and Las Bambas (and Ministro Hales offse-ng decline elsewhere at Codelco Norte). Taking into account a con-nued deple-on at exis-ng opera-ons, project slippage and other disrup-ons, the increase in mine output s-ll could be quite benign, at least un-l 2015. For now, we do see 2012 as a year of slight surplus, with growing surpluses to around 250 kt in 2014. We do also expect a much larger surplus in 2015 and 2016, as the project list indicates capacity growth of over 1.5 Mtpy in both years. A major earthquake hit central Chile on Sunday March 25th, measuring 7.1 on the richter scale. Although such high magnitude quakes can create major damage, Chile’s mines were reported to be opera-ng normally a-er the event. D. R. Congo: First Quantum is to receive US$1.25 billion from Kazakh miner ENRC in se-lement of the long-running dispute over the Kolwesi copper-cobalt tailings project, now in the hands of ENRC. According to the deal, first proposed in January, ENRC will acquire First Quantum’s residual claims and assets rela-ng to Kolwezi, Fron-er and Lonshi copper mines in Katanga province. The deal is subject to required third party consents and approvals and the se-lement of current interna-onal arbitra-ons concerning the assets.  Mineweb, March 2nd 2012. 

Anvil Mining Ltd. has reported that output at its flagship Kinsevere copper mine, has been affected by disrupted power supply. Indonesia: Opera-ons at Freeport McMoran’s Grasberg copper mine resumed on March 12th a-er their suspension on February 23rd as a result of rumbling labour disputes a-er a three-month strike affec-ng the mine last year. The recent dispute and security concerns related to the in-mida-on of employees that carried on working by those that had been on strike. The company, which s-ll maintains the force majeure imposed in October 2011 on some concentrate exports from the mine, now expects to produce 36.3 kt less copper and 125 koz less gold in the first quarter due to the labour ac-on. Under a new regula-on signed by President Yudhoyono, the Indonesian government plans to require foreign companies to sell stakes in mines they own in order to increase domes-c ownership to at least 51% by the tenth year of produc-on. According to Trade Minister Wirjawan the new regula-on would 

affect only short term investment. It was not clear how soon the regula-on, if imposed, will apply to exis-ng investments. The government is currently renego-a-ng exis-ng royalty contracts with major foreign mine owners, including copper miners Freeport McMoRan and Newmont Mining. Thomson Reuters, March 12th 2012.
